In [[mathematics]], especially [[general topology]] and [[mathematical analysis|analysis]], an '''exhaustion by compact sets'''{{sfn|Lee|2011|p=110}} of a [[topological space]] <math>X</math> is a nested [[sequence]] of [[compact subset]]s <math>K_i</math> of <math>X</math> (i.e. <math>K_1\subseteq K_2\subseteq K_3\subseteq\cdots</math>), 
such that each <math>K_i</math> is contained in the [[Interior (topology)|interior]] of <math>K_{i+1}</math>, i.e. <math>K_i\subset\text{int}(K_{i+1})</math>, and <math>X=\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty K_i</math>.

A space admitting an exhaustion by compact sets is called '''exhaustible by compact sets'''.{{sfn|Harder|2011|loc=Definition 4.4.10}}

As an example, for the space <math>X=\mathbb{R}^n</math>, the sequence of [[closed ball]]s <math>K_i = \{ x : |x| \le i \}</math> forms an exhaustion of the space by compact sets.

There is a weaker condition that drops the requirement that <math>K_i</math> is in the interior of <math>K_{i+1}</math>, meaning the space is [[σ-compact]] (i.e., a [[countable]] [[union (set theory)|union]] of compact subsets.)

== Construction ==
If there is an exhaustion by compact sets, the space is necessarily locally compact (if Hausdorff). The converse is also often true. For example, for a locally compact Hausdorff space <math>X</math> that is a countable union of compact subsets, we can construct an exhaustion as follows. We write <math>X = \bigcup_1^{\infty} K_n</math> as a union of compact sets <math>K_n</math>. Then inductively choose open sets <math>V_n \supset \overline{V_{n-1}} \cup K_n</math> with compact closures, where <math>V_0 = \emptyset</math>. Then <math>\overline{V_n}</math> is a required exhaustion.

For a locally compact Hausdorff space that is second-countable, a similar argument can be used to construct an exhaustion.

== Application ==
For a Hausdorff space <math>X</math>, an exhaustion by compact sets can be used to show the space is paracompact.<ref name="Warner">{{harvnb|Warner|1983|loc=Ch. 1. Lemma 1.9.}}</ref> Indeed, suppose we have an increasing sequence <math>V_1 \subset V_2 \subset \cdots </math> of open subsets such that <math>X = \bigcup V_n</math> and each <math>\overline{V_n}</math> is compact and is contained in <math>V_{n+1}</math>. Let <math>\mathcal{U}</math> be an open cover of <math>X</math>. We also let <math>V_n = \emptyset, \, n \le 0</math>. Then, for each <math>n \ge 1</math>, <math>\{ (V_{n + 1} - \overline{V_{n-2}}) \cap U \mid U \in \mathcal{U} \}</math> is an open cover of the compact set <math>\overline{V_n} - V_{n-1}</math> and thus admits a finite subcover <math>\mathcal{V}_n</math>. Then <math>\mathcal{V} := \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} \mathcal{V}_n</math> is a locally finite refinement of <math>\mathcal{U}.</math>

Remark: The proof in fact shows that each open cover admits a countable refinement consisting of open sets with compact closures and each of whose members intersects only finitely many others.<ref name="Warner" />

The following type of converse also holds. A paracompact locally compact Hausdorff space with countably many open connected components is a countable union of compact sets<ref>{{harvnb|Wall|2016|loc=Proposition A.2.8. (ii)}} NB: the proof in the reference looks problematic. It can be fixed by constructing an open cover whose member intersects only finitely many others. (Then we use the fact that a locally finite connected graph is countable.) </ref> and thus admits an exhaustion by compact subsets.

== Relation to other properties ==

The following are equivalent for a topological space <math>X</math>:<ref>{{cite web |title=A question about local compactness and $\sigma$-compactness |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/q/2078142 |website=Mathematics Stack Exchange}}</ref>

# <math>X</math> is exhaustible by compact sets.
# <math>X</math> is [[σ-compact]] and [[weakly locally compact]].
# <math>X</math> is [[Lindelöf (topology)|Lindelöf]] and weakly locally compact.
(where ''weakly locally compact'' means [[locally compact]] in the weak sense that each point has a compact [[neighborhood (mathematics)|neighborhood]]).

The [[hemicompact]] property is intermediate between exhaustible by compact sets and σ-compact.  Every space exhaustible by compact sets is hemicompact<ref>{{cite web |title=Does locally compact and $\sigma$-compact non-Hausdorff space imply hemicompact? |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/a/4569500/52912 |website=Mathematics Stack Exchange}}</ref> and every hemicompact space is σ-compact, but the [[converse (logic)|reverse implications]] do not hold.  For example, the [[Arens-Fort space]] and the [[Appert space]] are hemicompact, but not exhaustible by compact sets (because not weakly locally compact),<ref>{{cite web |title=Can a hemicompact space fail to be weakly locally compact? |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4566624 |website=Mathematics Stack Exchange}}</ref> and the set <math>\Q</math> of [[rational number]]s with the usual [[topological space|topology]] is σ-compact, but not hemicompact.<ref>{{cite web |title=A $\sigma$-compact but not hemicompact space? |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4209303 |website=Mathematics Stack Exchange}}</ref>

Every [[regular Hausdorff space]] that is a countable union of compact sets is [[paracompact]].{{fact|date=November 2024}}<!-- Even though such a space does not admit an exhaustion by compact subsets? as far as I can tell, this statement is not proved in the reference. {{cite web |title=locally compact and sigma-compact spaces are paracompact in nLab |url=https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/locally+compact+and+sigma-compact+spaces+are+paracompact |website=ncatlab.org}}</ref> -->
